tweets.text:
Hmm. I might ask @dylan522p if Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) is compatible with data locality and not moving the KV cache. That constraint is what OpenAI focused on with Jalapeño. They absolutely did not make an “explicit bet that disagg is not the way to go.” There are multiple forms of disaggregation, and one disaggregated topology compatible with data locality is prefill and attention computed on Jalapeño and FFN on another chip.
 
And they are obviously doing relatively crude disaggregated inference (PD) at scale today with their GPU fleet. Today. 
 
AFD is a hard networking problem that everyone is working on as it can be generally superior to simpler PD disaggregation via approaching similar interactivity without making the traditional tradeoffs between latency and throughput for growing KV caches.
 
The CS-4 Wafer I/O Module was described as a “programmable, universal disaggregation interface” designed to support multiple forms of disaggregation, including both prefill-decode disaggregation and attention-FFN disaggregation.
 
We know that CS-4 is capable of crude PD disaggregation today with GPUs (Helios) and the Trainiums. Likely already generating tokens today in one - and probably both - of these setups.
 
And I think this is about as explicit a statement as one will get from a public company about Jalapeño and its potential FFN disaggregation companion chip. “Jalapeño+Cerebras.”
 
And if can do AFD disaggregation with Jalapeño then can almost certainly do it with Trainiums and at a minimum Helios GPUs. We keep treating privacy scandals like isolated events.

But history shows us an obvious pattern of how control over personal data has shifted away from us.

These past events show it clearly:

1. Patriot Act (2001): Expanded US surveillance powers after 9/11 and later became the basis for bulk collection of Americans’ phone records.

2. Snowden disclosures (2013): Revealed that the NSA had been collecting phone and communications data at a massive scale.

3. Apple vs FBI (2016): The FBI tried to force Apple to create software that could bypass the security of a locked iPhone.

4. UK Investigatory Powers Act (2016): Gave UK authorities broad powers to intercept communications, collect data in bulk, and hack devices.

5. Cambridge Analytica (2018): Data originating from a Facebook quiz ultimately exposed information tied to as many as 87M people. This is the one I talked about in a previous post.

Btw, all of these events are documented and preserved on @Logos_network's Systems of Control Exhibition.

I think it's a great initiative to keep those records alive. I wouldn't want them fading into another old headline.

It's time we put some effort into preserving our own data and privacy.

Disclosure: I'm a big supporter of Logos' privacy efforts.

I thought this would be a good time to address what actually is address poisoning.

Essentially, an attacker sends you a tiny amount of crypto from a wallet address that looks almost identical to one you’ve used before.

The goal is to get their address into your transaction history and hope you copy it the next time you send funds.

And that's exactly what happened here.

After withdrawing funds from @compoundfinance, the victim received a 0.0002 USDC dust transaction from a spoofed address.

Later, when they went to move around $2M, they appear to have copied that fake address from their history instead of the real one.

It's a very expensive copy/paste mistake. So here's something you can do to protect yourself:

→ Don’t copy addresses from your transaction history
→ Use a saved address book where possible
→ Check more than the first and last few characters
→ For a big transfer, always do a test transaction first

I know a lot of these things sound obvious, but fraudsters are counting on people moving fast and not checking every detail. Don’t give them that advantage.

China’s AI hardware disadvantage is turning efficiency into a competitive advantage.

Chinese labs have spent the past several years trying to keep pace with the frontier under tighter restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Restricted access made it harder to improve models by simply adding more compute. Labs had to look for gains in how models were trained and run.

Much of that work focuses on improving chip utilization during training and designing models that require less compute and memory. Post-training methods are also extracting more reasoning capability from existing base models.

Chinese AI progress cannot be reduced to distillation. These systems change how models are built and run while lowering training and serving costs.

That cost advantage changes how models compete. Many workloads do not require the strongest model available. A lower-cost option can win once it performs well enough for the task. Several Chinese models already combine competitive performance with substantially lower prices.

China is much closer to running competitive models on domestic chips than it is to training them from scratch. Frontier training still depends on advanced hardware China cannot yet fully replace. The next generation of Chinese models will show how far better software and more efficient architectures can narrow that gap.

The biggest catalysts I see for Collector Crypt over the next few months as one of their early investors:

1) The CLARITY Act and increasing regulatory clarity.

Collector Crypt is probably THE project with the most attractive ratio of revenue generation to market cap out there, and the reason for that is that people have doubts about what they're actually buying with the token. Increasing regulatory clarity will clear those doubts out of the way and lead to a massive repricing. Those who put in the work now and decide for themselves how committed and trustable this team really is should benefit from that repricing, and from the massive discount available right now.

On top of that, I'm firmly convinced it will be a huge edge for Collector down the line that they're specifically NOT burning 50-100% of their revenue on buybacks just to keep token holders and short term community members happy. Instead they reinvest it into the business to strengthen their market position and compound massively over time.

2) The Pokemon 30th anniversary is coming up next month.

I think it's going to get really loud around Pokemon and TCGs again, both inside and outside of crypto. How could Collector Crypt not benefit from that.

3) The CARDS 1 year anniversary is also coming up next month.

They've already announced the return of their "gacha games," which was a big success before, and I wouldn't be surprised if there are more surprises lined up, especially as it aligns with the Pokemon anniversary. Expect this to bring significant attention, users and volume back to both their gacha and their secondary marketplace.

4) They have a massive new product release coming up in October.

I want to avoid saying too much, as it's highly confidential and they obviously want to remain competitive, but a few community members have already connected the dots and hinted at it. If you do some digging, you should be able to do the same.

What I can say is that it will be a completely new product offering at a huge scale. I'm confident this will not only bring Collector Crypt to a huge number of non-crypto people and finally make it grow outside of this crypto echo chamber without people even realizing it, but at the same time bring huge amounts of supply onchain. I wish I could say more, but I strongly believe this will be the key differentiating factor for Collector Crypt to establish itself as the absolute incumbent, hit escape velocity, and grow at an unprecedented speed.

5) Overall market conditions.

While I'm excited that they'll soon build market share outside of crypto too, the crypto native business is still hugely important. I was impressed by the volume crypto natives already drove on the platform during a bear market, so I don't even want to imagine the kind of volume they'll drive in a bull market, when everyone has made money and is far more willing to spend it loosely on things they love.

To sum it up: I think the current $CARDS prices are an absolute blessing for anyone willing to do some research, and for those willing to think a bit longer term than 2 days.

Sure, I might be biased here, as I'm an early investor in Collector Crypt. For what it's worth, we still hold our venture position despite the fact it's fully unlocked already, and bought even more on the liquid market. But that's also exactly why I'm close to the team and speak with them regularly, so I genuinely feel comfortable vouching for this team, their trustworthiness, and their commitment to their token holders.

@TuomHolmberg will probably hate me for this tweet, but it's time for people to wake up to what might be one of the most underpriced assets and greatest onchain businesses in the entire industry.

"To understand the implications for SocialFi, let's first examine the dynamics of Web2:

Traditional social media, undeniably one of the most utilized aspects of the internet, succeeds through an obvious flywheel. Social innovation often goes viral quickly, leading to the emergence of new KOLs. This chance for virality attracts a large number of users, driven by the hope of fame and attention.

The dopamine rush from engagement, likes, and impressions - probably the most consumed drug of the 21st century.

This influx of users then draws existing KOLs, who are motivated by both the opportunity to reach a new audience and the fear of becoming irrelevant. This, in turn, lends more credibility to the platform, accelerating user onboarding. As this positive feedback loop continues, the network effects strengthen, creating a moat and increasing user stickiness.

WE ARE HERE RIGHT NOW WITH FOMO

However, as users' attention spans shorten and their patience wanes, platform operators face significant pressure to evolve, ideally leading to further social innovation and restarting the cycle.

Instagram, we all remember its early days. It started out as a simple tool to capture, edit, and share images with your followers. Quickly, it became a staple on everyone’s phone. But like any successful platform, Instagram had to evolve to stay relevant.

In 2016, driven by the relentless surge in Snapchat's Stories popularity, Instagram faced mounting pressure to adapt. Responding to this competitive threat, Instagram launched its own version, not just mimicking the feature but even adopting the same name. This strategic move was a direct effort to retain user engagement and stay relevant in the dynamic social media landscape.

And this was just the beginning. They soon integrated an algorithmic feed to help users discover content more easily and capture their attention even more efficiently. Not long after, Reels emerged as a direct response to TikTok’s explosive popularity.

The message from Instagram’s evolution is clear: Copy and bundle innovation of others rather than being left behind."

SocialFi was always meant to be THE non-institutional use case to onboard hundreds of millions of users onchain. And while I'm completely sidelined on fomo, I'll be rooting for their success, because it won't just make the pie grow again, it'll multiply it by orders of magnitude.

Keep the flywheel spinning.

this is an awesome way of finding customers.

here’s how you can run the full workflow by creating a buyer intent agent with hermes today: 👇 

1: Turn on the tools

> Run hermes tools.
> Enable X Search.
> Enable Web Search + Extract.
> Enable Browser.
> Enable Files.
> Enable Cron / scheduled tasks.

Hermes’ X search is read-only and can use SuperGrok/X Premium+ OAuth or an xAI API key. 

2: Create the Buyer Intent Agent

> Create a Buyer Intent Agent.
> Give it X Search + Web Search + Browser + Files.
> Tell it its only job is finding people publicly showing buying intent.

3: Tell it what you sell

Give Hermes:

> Your product.
> Your competitors.
> The problems you solve.
> Your ideal customer.
> Bad-fit customers to ignore.

Example:

“We sell X.
Competitors are A, B and C.
Target founders and marketing leads at companies with 5–100 employees.”

4: Search X for pain

Tell it to search the last 7 days for:

> “alternative to [competitor]”
> “switching from [competitor]”
> “[competitor] is too expensive”
> “hate [competitor]”
> “[competitor] is frustrating”
> “what should I use instead of [competitor]”
> Direct complaints about the problem you solve.

Hermes has a dedicated x_search tool for public posts and threads. 

5: Mine the replies too

For every good post:

> Read the thread.
> Find replies agreeing with the complaint.
> Find people saying they have the same problem.
> Treat them as separate potential leads.

So one complaint might produce 5-10 prospects instead of one.

6: Remove rubbish

Tell Hermes:

> Ignore bots.
> Ignore obvious spam.
> Ignore competitor employees.
> Ignore joke posts.
> Ignore old complaints.
> Ignore people who clearly cannot buy the product.

7: Research each person

For every remaining lead:

> Search their name.
> Read their X bio.
> Find their role.
> Find their company.
> Find their company website.
> Never guess missing information.

8: Research their company

> What does the company do?
> Roughly how large is it?
> What industry is it in?
> Does it match our ICP?
> Could this person influence buying the product?

This can also replace what Amplemarket was doing but their job is to make it easier for you.

9: Score every lead

Give Hermes a simple score:

> Pain: /10
> Buying intent: /10
> ICP fit: /10
> Authority: /10
> Recency: /10

Then:

> Rank the strongest leads first.
> Drop weak leads.
> Only keep prospects above your chosen score.

10: Save everything

Simplest version:

> Create buyer-intent-leads.csv.
> Add each new lead as a row.
> Never add duplicates.

Columns:

> Name
> X account
> Company
> Role
> Original post
> Complaint
> Date
> Intent score
> ICP score
> Reason it matters
> Status

Hermes can read, search, create and edit local files itself. 

Move it to Google Sheets later.

11: Draft personalised outreach

For every strong lead:

> Read their exact complaint.
> Write a short public reply.
> Write a short DM.
> Reference what they actually said.
> Never use generic sales language.

For example:

“Saw your post about X being painful on Mac. We built Y specifically around that problem…”

12: Keep sending manual

Add this permanent rule:

“Never post, DM or email anyone without my approval.”

13: Test it

First say:

“Find me 20 buyer-intent leads from X from the last 7 days using this workflow.”

Then inspect the results. If they’re poor:

> Correct the scoring.
> Add exclusions.
> Improve search phrases.
> Tighten your ICP.

Do this until the leads are genuinely good.

14: Turn it into a Skill

Once it works:

> Ask Hermes to save the process as a Buyer Intent Skill.
> Include your searches, filters, scoring system and output format.

This means you don’t have to explain the whole workflow every time.

15: Make it automatic

Just ask it to schedule what you want!

Being dependent on Canada and being exposed to tariffs are now two different things.

The U.S. has cycled through tariff authorities all year. The Supreme Court struck down the emergency-powers tariffs in February. A temporary global tariff expired in July. The administration has since reached for a 1930 statute to impose 50% duties on selected Canadian goods.

But even before that latest round took effect, the tariff landscape was already a patchwork — aluminum and steel heavily tariffed, energy barely touched, everything else somewhere in between. Which means the states most tied to Canada aren't necessarily the states most exposed to auto tariffs.

Most dependent on Canada: Montana 91%, Vermont 70%, Maine 69%, North Dakota 68%, Wyoming 49% Largest Canadian auto exposure: Michigan, Texas, West Virginia, Missouri, Ohio

Almost no overlap.

Montana gets 91% of its imports from Canada, and almost none of it is vehicles. Michigan gets 26% from Canada — but more than half of that is vehicles and parts. Canadian vehicles and auto parts represent roughly 14% of everything Michigan imports — about 10x the national average.

Montana is more than three times as dependent on Canada overall, but has only a fraction of Michigan's exposure to the auto trade. Even inside autos, states are exposed through different doors.

Kentucky is a parts state — roughly a fifth of what it imports from Canada is auto parts, with very few finished vehicles. Texas is almost the reverse — a large share of its Canadian imports are finished vehicles, with relatively few parts.

Michigan is deep in both.

A tariff on parts and a tariff on finished vehicles hit two different maps. And whatever comes next won't hit evenly either.

Montana, Vermont and Maine look relatively insulated from the auto fight. But much of their Canadian exposure runs through energy, wood and other commodities. By June, the effective tariff rate on Canadian wood had already risen from near zero to 4.6%. They're not insulated. They're exposed to a different line item.

$SNAP 𝗦𝗕𝗖: 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗣𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗧 𝗜𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗢𝗢𝗠

A lot of the criticism around $SNAP starts with stock-based compensation, and that criticism is fair. SBC is still high.

What I don’t agree with is the idea, repeated quite often on X, that Evan Spiegel has no incentive to see the stock go higher because he is simply using Snap as his personal piggy bank.

The facts point in the opposite direction.

SBC as a percentage of revenue has been steadily improving:

2023: ~29%
2024: ~19%
2025: ~17%
H1 2026: ~16%

More importantly, Spiegel himself has not been taking massive new stock grants. His billionaire status comes primarily from the Snap shares he already owns. Remove those shares and his net worth is likely measured in hundreds of millions, not billions.

Over the past three years, Evan Spiegel has received about $10.9 million in total reported compensation from Snap, virtually all of it security and travel-related benefits. He received $3 in total salary and $0 in new stock awards.

His economic incentive is therefore very simple: the higher $SNAP goes, the wealthier he becomes. If the stock continues falling, a large part of his wealth falls with it.

The problem has never really been Spiegel extracting billions from the company. The problem has been the company itself: too many employees, too much spending, excessive company-wide SBC and too much money directed toward projects that produced little shareholder value.

And that is exactly what makes Snap such an unusual investment situation.

Most companies in the stock market would probably envy this problem.

They need to invent new products, enter new markets, beat competitors or create new sources of revenue just to materially improve their economics.

Snap may not need to do much of that.

It mainly needs to stop doing what is unnecessary.

The process has already started. Snap recently cut roughly 16% of its workforce, around 1,000 employees, and eliminated more than 300 open positions. Management expects those actions to reduce its annualized cost base by more than $500 million by the second half of 2026.

AI provides another major tailwind. Smaller teams can increasingly do work that previously required much larger organizations. For a company where a large portion of SBC comes from R&D, that matters.

The investment case therefore doesn’t require heroic assumptions.

If revenue keeps growing while headcount, expenses and SBC continue falling as a percentage of revenue, operating leverage can improve very quickly.

That is Snap’s unusual position.

Most struggling companies need to figure out what they should start doing.

Snap may already have the product, the users and the revenue growth it needs.

It mostly needs to figure out what to stop doing.

And with an activist investor now in the room, there is finally another adult pushing management toward exactly that conclusion.

The biggest catalyst for $SNAP may not be what it creates next.

It may be what it finally stops wasting money on.

I keep getting asked: “How long are you planning to hold this stock?”

It’s a question I can’t really answer.

Imagine you just started dating someone and I ask, “How long are you going to stay with her?”

You’d probably say: I don’t know. Let’s see.

She looks good, acts well, talks well. That’s the initial thesis. But then you learn more. How does she behave with your parents? How does she treat people? How does she react when things don’t go her way?

Any one of those things can change the thesis.

Stocks are the same.

I could be out of $SNAP next quarter, even at $5, if I see that things are not developing the way I expected.

Or I could still be holding it at $20 if Evan Spiegel and management are actually making the changes I believe could unlock value.

Maybe you hold for a month. Maybe a year. Maybe ten years.

The holding period isn’t decided when I buy.

The thesis is.
And I hold for as long as the facts continue to support it.

𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗙𝗢𝗟𝗜𝗢

Watch the Peter Lynch video below.

There have only been a handful of investors in history who consistently beat the market over very long periods.

Peter Lynch and Stanley Druckenmiller are probably somewhere in the top five, arguably top three.

And both have said versions of the same thing about concentration.

One of my biggest realizations over the last four years is that when I find an unusually obvious opportunity, I’m not afraid to concentrate.

I’m not saying you should wake up tomorrow and put 40% into a stock. Opportunities that justify that kind of concentration may come once a year, or once every two years.

But if you have done the work, understand the risks, and genuinely believe you have one of your best ideas in front of you, then owning 2% or 3% almost defeats the purpose.

If your best ideas are never at least 10% of your portfolio, you may be spending an enormous amount of time researching without allowing your best work to meaningfully affect your returns.

When I had around 40% in $ZIM, people called it reckless. But I was looking at a profitable company trading below the cash it held, with additional assets on top.

For me, taking money away from that opportunity simply to buy companies I understood much less, just for the sake of diversification, would have made even less sense.

People often point to hedge funds owning 40 or 50 stocks. But large funds have teams of analysts. Each analyst may really have only three or four highest-conviction ideas. Put 10 analysts together and suddenly the fund owns 40 stocks.

That is very different from one person pretending to deeply understand 40 companies.

Of course, this does not apply equally to every industry.

Biotech is a good example. Many biotech investments are closer to hero-or-zero outcomes, where one trial, one FDA decision or one safety issue can completely change the value of the company. In that kind of sector, diversification matters much more.

Concentration makes the most sense when you can actually understand and control the major variables of the thesis.

And when you really have an edge, your position has to be large enough for that edge to actually matter.

𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗙𝗢𝗟𝗜𝗢

Watch the Peter Lynch video below.

There have only been a handful of investors in history who consistently beat the market over very long periods.

Peter Lynch and Stanley Druckenmiller are probably somewhere in the top five, arguably top three.

And both have said versions of the same thing about concentration.

One of my biggest realizations over the last four years is that when I find an unusually obvious opportunity, I’m not afraid to concentrate.

I’m not saying you should wake up tomorrow and put 40% into a stock. Opportunities that justify that kind of concentration may come once a year, or once every two years.

But if you have done the work, understand the risks, and genuinely believe you have one of your best ideas in front of you, then owning 2% or 3% almost defeats the purpose.

If your best ideas are never at least 10% of your portfolio, you may be spending an enormous amount of time researching without allowing your best work to meaningfully affect your returns.

When I had around 40% in $ZIM, people called it reckless. But I was looking at a profitable company trading below the cash it held, with additional assets on top.

For me, taking money away from that opportunity simply to buy companies I understood much less, just for the sake of diversification, would have made even less sense.

People often point to hedge funds owning 40 or 50 stocks. But large funds have teams of analysts. Each analyst may really have only three or four highest-conviction ideas. Put 10 analysts together and suddenly the fund owns 40 stocks.

That is very different from one person pretending to deeply understand 40 companies.

Of course, this does not apply equally to every industry.

Biotech is a good example. Many biotech investments are closer to hero-or-zero outcomes, where one trial, one FDA decision or one safety issue can completely change the value of the company. In that kind of sector, diversification matters much more.

Concentration makes the most sense when you can actually understand and control the major variables of the thesis.

And when you really have an edge, your position has to be large enough for that edge to actually matter.

I was stuck in traffic in an Uber. Two hours. Couldn't move.

I realized the driver was the same one I'd had months ago.

Back then, I'd told him about AI music and showed him a song. He loved it.

Six months later, in that traffic jam, he reminded me. Then he said: "So I started playing around with it."

He played us the best music. This incredible vibe of meshing two cultures. Unbelievably fabulous.

It kept us interested the entire time we were stuck.

That's AI spreading. That's an artist thinking: "Now we've got AI, what do we do with it?"

Not "AI is going to take my job."

It's "I got to use AI. I got to be a better musician."

AI is just the new guitar.

Some artists will resist it. Some will master it.

Those who master it will create things we can't yet imagine.

By the way, that driver? He's proof that AI democratizes creativity. Anyone with curiosity and access can make something extraordinary.
